newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians resolve dispute over diplomatic posts.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians resolve dispute over diplomatic posts.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke said on Friday that rival Bosnian leaders resolved a dispute over the distribution of ambassadorial posts which triggered an international diplomatic freeze on the country's envoys.

Under the deal, the Bosnian envoy to the United Nations would be a Moslem, a Serb would be appointed as ambassador to Washington and a Croat would serve as envoy to Japan, Holbrooke and other mediators told reporters.

Members of the multi-ethnic collective presidency also agreed on the composition of a joint military commission and on a single area code for the country's peacetime telephone network, said Holbrooke, the architect of Bosnia's 1995 peace agreement.
"These agreements are full evidence of Western determination (to enforce the peace agreement)," Holbrooke told reporters. "These are steps forward and pretty solid ones."

The United States and European countries had suspended contacts this week with Bosnian envoys after Moslem, Croat and Serb political leaders failed to agree how to divide 33 diplomatic posts by an August 1 deadline set by major powers.
German diplomat Gerd Wagner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, said he would recommend to major powers on Friday to lift the suspension on diplomatic contacts.

Bosnian's current ambassadors were appointed by the wartime Moslem-led Bosnian government which fought for independence against separatist Serb forces and, for 10 months, Croat forces, their nominal allies.
Serb and Croat leaders had complained that the Moslems, who comprise the largest ethnic community in Bosnia, were dominating the diplomatic service despite promises to share power equally.
Moslem representatives feared that Serb or Croat nationalist parties would undermine Bosnia's statehood by appointing hardliners to ambassadorial posts.

The leaders agreed that 13 ambassadors would be Moslem, 11 Serb and eight Croat and one would be jointly appointed by the Moslem chairman of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic and the Croat member, Kresimir Zubak.
Bosnian Moslem officials said the presidency members failed to agree on the design of a joint currency, dealing a setback to efforts to clinch an agreement with the International Monetary Fund.
Serb presidency member Momcilo Krajisnik insisted on the use of nationalist symbols on the currency which offended his Moslem and Croat counterparts, officials said.
